title: Data Warehousing & OLAP
summary: Analytics at scale: why a separate warehouse exists, how ETL feeds it, and how star schemas and OLAP cubes make aggregate queries fast.

blocks.markdown:
A **data warehouse** is a separate database built for analytics — not for running your app.

- Operational databases handle daily transactions; warehouses answer questions like "revenue by region last quarter."
- Data is copied in, cleaned, and pre-organized so big aggregations run fast.
- The query style is called **OLAP** (Online Analytical Processing).
- Key artifacts: star schema, fact/dimension tables, ETL pipelines.

Two fundamentally different query workloads.

| | OLTP | OLAP |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Run the business | Analyze the business |
| Queries | Short, indexed row lookups | Long scans across millions of rows |
| Schema | Normalized (3NF) | Denormalized (star/snowflake) |

**OLTP** (Online Transaction Processing) = your app's live database (orders, logins). **OLAP** = your analytics warehouse.

Running heavy analytics on your operational DB hurts everyone.

- A full-table scan for a quarterly report locks rows and slows inserts for live users.
- Operational schema is normalized for writes, not for the wide reads analytics needs.
- Warehouses are optimized differently: **columnar storage**, different indexes, no FK enforcement.
- Separating them lets each do its job without interference. See [database-design](database-design).

Data flows from sources, through a transformation layer, into the warehouse, then out to reports.

<<< Image: a left-to-right pipeline with four labeled boxes connected by arrows: 'Operational DBs / APIs / Files' → 'ETL / ELT' → 'Data Warehouse' → 'BI Tools / Reports'. Clean, blue-grey palette, generous whitespace, 2-3 word labels only. >>>

- **Sources**: CRMs, transactional DBs, flat files, event streams.
- **ETL/ELT**: extract, clean, and load data on a schedule (hourly, nightly).
- **Warehouse**: the central store, organized for analytics.
- **BI tools**: Tableau, Looker, custom dashboards — query the warehouse.

blocks.subTitle: The building blocks
blocks.markdown:
Every warehouse schema splits data into two roles.

- **Fact table** — stores measurable events: a sale, a click, a payment. Rows are narrow and numerous (billions). Columns are metrics (amount, quantity) and foreign keys to dimension tables.
- **Dimension table** — stores context: who, what, where, when. Rows are wide and few (thousands). Example: a `Product` dimension with name, category, brand.

A query joins a fact table to one or more dimensions to answer "total sales by product category." See [normalization](normalization).

The **star schema** is the standard warehouse layout: one central fact table surrounded by flat dimension tables, like a star.

<<< Image: a central rectangle labeled 'Fact: Sales' with foreign-key columns listed, surrounded by four rectangles labeled 'Dim: Date', 'Dim: Product', 'Dim: Customer', 'Dim: Store', each connected by a single arrow to the center. Star arrangement, blue-grey palette, generous whitespace. >>>

- Dimensions are **denormalized** — all attributes in one table, no further joins needed.
- Simple to query: join fact to any dimension in one hop.
- Trades some redundancy for query speed.

blocks.subTitle: vs Snowflake schema
blocks.markdown:
The **snowflake schema** normalizes dimension tables into sub-dimensions.

| | Star | Snowflake |
|---|---|---|
| Dimensions | Flat, denormalized | Normalized, split tables |
| Query joins | Few (1 hop) | More (2+ hops) |
| Storage | More redundancy | Less redundancy |

Star = simpler queries, slightly larger; snowflake = less storage, more complex JOINs. Star wins in most BI workloads because query speed matters more than storage.

How data gets from sources into the warehouse.

- **ETL** (Extract → Transform → Load): transform data in a staging area *before* loading. Traditional; keeps the warehouse clean.
- **ELT** (Extract → Load → Transform): load raw data first, transform *inside* the warehouse using its own compute. Modern approach used by BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift — their compute is cheap and scalable.

ELT is now the default for cloud warehouses; ETL is still common when strong data governance is required.

Aggregating billions of rows on every query is slow. Two techniques pre-compute results.

- **Materialized view**: a query whose result is stored on disk and refreshed on schedule. Query hits the stored result, not the raw table. See [sql-objects](sql-objects).
- **Pre-aggregation (OLAP cube)**: sums and counts computed for every combination of dimensions (date × region × product) and stored. Queries answer in milliseconds.

Trade-off: pre-aggregation speeds reads but costs storage and refresh time.

A **data lake** stores raw, unprocessed data from all sources in one place — no schema enforced at write time.

- Format: flat files (Parquet, JSON, CSV) on cheap object storage (S3, GCS).
- Schema is applied at read time (schema-on-read) by the query engine.
- Use case: keep everything; decide later what to structure.

A data warehouse is curated and fast; a data lake is cheap and flexible. Many teams use both: lake for raw storage, warehouse for the cleaned, queryable layer.

**Data mining** is finding non-obvious patterns in large datasets.

- Common tasks: **classification** (label new records), **clustering** (group similar records), **association rules** (items bought together), **anomaly detection** (flag outliers).
- The warehouse is the input; mining sits on top.
- In practice, data mining is now called **ML / data science** — the concepts are the same, the tooling evolved.

Common mistakes in warehouse design:

- **Running analytics on the OLTP DB.** Even read-only queries lock shared resources and degrade app performance.
- **Over-normalizing the warehouse.** Snowflake schema feels clean but adds costly joins at query time; prefer star.
- **Stale materialized views.** Forgetting to schedule refreshes means dashboards show yesterday's numbers as if current.
- **Treating the data lake as the warehouse.** Raw storage is not a substitute for structured, queryable data.

blocks.subTitle: Schema design trap
blocks.markdown: **Confusing fact and dimension columns.** A fact table stores *events* (one row per sale); a dimension stores *context* (one row per product). Putting descriptive attributes like product name in the fact table bloats it and defeats the star design — billions of rows with repeated strings instead of a single FK.

blocks.subTitle: OLTP vs OLAP
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP?**

**OLTP** runs the live application — short, indexed reads/writes on individual rows (an order insert, a login check). **OLAP** answers analytical questions — long scans aggregating millions of rows (revenue by region). OLTP is normalized; OLAP is denormalized into star/snowflake schemas and lives in a separate warehouse so analytics don't impact app performance.

blocks.subTitle: Why a separate warehouse
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why keep analytics off the operational database?**

Heavy scans on the OLTP DB contend with live transactions for CPU, I/O, and locks — degrading app performance. The warehouse uses columnar storage and denormalized schemas optimized for reads, which the normalized OLTP schema cannot efficiently provide. Separation also means schema changes for analytics don't risk the live system.

blocks.subTitle: Star vs snowflake schema
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Star schema vs snowflake schema — which would you pick and why?**

**Star**: dimensions are denormalized flat tables; one join from fact to any dimension. **Snowflake**: dimensions are normalized into sub-tables; fewer duplicate values but more joins. For BI workloads, star wins — query simplicity and speed matter more than the small storage saving. Snowflake schema is useful when dimensions are very large and updates are frequent.

blocks.subTitle: Fact vs dimension table
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the difference between a fact table and a dimension table?**

A **fact table** records events (sales, clicks) and contains metrics (amount, count) plus foreign keys. It is tall and narrow — billions of rows. A **dimension table** records context (product, customer, date) and is wide and short — thousands of rows with descriptive attributes. Queries join fact to dimensions to slice metrics by context.

blocks.subTitle: ETL vs ELT
blocks.markdown:
**Q: ETL vs ELT — what changed and why?**

**ETL** transforms data in a staging area before loading — traditional, clean, but slow when data volumes grow. **ELT** loads raw data first, then transforms inside the warehouse. Modern cloud warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift) have elastic compute, so running transforms inside them is fast and cheap. ELT is now the default; ETL remains when strict pre-load governance is required.
